plain_language_explanation: The patient is a woman in her 30s who needs contraception but cannot tolerate hormonal methods. Her doctor prescribed Phexxi, a non-hormonal vaginal gel contraceptive. The health insurer denied coverage, stating that Phexxi is not medically necessary. The patient has already tried and failed multiple types of birth control: several oral contraceptive pills, Gynol II (a spermicidal jelly), Shur Seal (a contraceptive gel), and a diaphragm.

recommended_strategy: The appeal should emphasize that the patient has exhausted multiple contraceptive options across both hormonal and non-hormonal categories, and that Phexxi is an FDA-approved non-hormonal contraceptive medically appropriate for her situation. Key arguments: (1) Document that hormonal methods are not an option due to intolerance; (2) List all failed non-hormonal methods already tried; (3) Request the plan identify any remaining covered non-hormonal alternatives it believes should be tried first, and be prepared to explain contraindications or prior failures if such alternatives exist; (4) Cite the ACA and New York contraceptive coverage mandates; (5) Argue that denying all remaining contraceptive options effectively denies the patient access to contraception altogether, which may violate coverage mandates. Request the plan's specific written medical necessity criteria for Phexxi and explain how the patient meets them or why those criteria are arbitrary if they exclude patients who have failed other methods.
draft_appeal:
Dear [Plan Name] Appeals Department:

Re: Appeal of Denial for Phexxi (vaginal gel contraceptive)
Patient: [Patient Name]
Claim Number: [Claim Number]
Date of Denial: [Date]

I am writing to appeal your denial of coverage for Phexxi 1.8-1-0.4% vaginal gel. Your denial letter stated that Phexxi is "not medically necessary." I respectfully disagree and request that you reverse this denial.

MEDICAL NECESSITY

I am a woman in my 30s who requires effective contraception. I have an intolerance to hormonal contraceptive methods, which eliminates birth control pills, patches, rings, shots, and hormonal IUDs as options for me. My healthcare provider has documented my intolerance to hormonal methods.

I have tried multiple oral contraceptives, all of which I could not tolerate. Additionally, I have tried the following non-hormonal barrier methods, all of which failed:
• Gynol II (spermicidal jelly)
• Shur Seal (contraceptive gel)
• Diaphragm

My healthcare provider has submitted a letter documenting my trial history and supporting the medical necessity of Phexxi as an appropriate non-hormonal contraceptive option for me.

Phexxi is FDA-approved as a non-hormonal, on-demand contraceptive. It is medically appropriate for patients like me who cannot use hormonal methods and have not succeeded with other barrier methods.

COVERAGE OBLIGATIONS

Under the Affordable Care Act and New York insurance law, health plans must cover FDA-approved contraceptives without cost-sharing. By denying Phexxi after I have failed or cannot tolerate other covered options, the plan is effectively denying me access to contraception.

REQUEST FOR INFORMATION

If you believe there are other non-hormonal contraceptive methods I should try before Phexxi is covered, please identify them specifically. Please also provide your written medical necessity criteria for Phexxi so I can understand what documentation would satisfy your requirements.

REQUEST FOR RELIEF

I respectfully request that you:
1. Reverse the denial and approve coverage for Phexxi
2. Provide coverage retroactive to the original prescription date
3. If you uphold the denial, provide a detailed written explanation of what additional clinical information or trials would be required for approval

I have exhausted the contraceptive options available to me. Phexxi is medically necessary and appropriate. I ask that you approve this appeal.

Sincerely,
[Patient Signature]

Enclosures: Provider letter documenting trial history and medical necessity

procedural_route.details: This case is from New York Department of Financial Services External Appeal system, indicating the patient has already completed an internal appeal and proceeded to external review. For future similar situations in New York: insurers must decide internal appeals within specific timeframes (typically 30 days for non-urgent, 72 hours for urgent pre-service, 48 hours for urgent concurrent). If the internal appeal is denied, the patient may request external review through NY DFS. The external review process in NY does not have a patient-paid filing fee for most cases. However, because this packet represents a case that has already reached external review, specific deadlines for the next procedural step are not applicable—the external review decision would already have been rendered. For someone in a similar initial position: they would need to file an internal appeal within 180 days of an adverse determination, and then request external review within four months of receiving a final internal adverse determination.

outcome_estimate.reasons: The outcome depends heavily on information not in the packet: (1) whether the plan has specific step-therapy requirements or formulary restrictions for Phexxi; (2) whether there are other non-hormonal alternatives the plan considers untried (particularly copper IUD); (3) the specific clinical documentation of hormone intolerance severity; and (4) how external reviewers weigh ACA/NY contraceptive coverage mandates against plan-specific medical necessity criteria. Strengths: documented failures of multiple methods across categories, provider support, and regulatory presumption favoring contraceptive coverage. Weaknesses: lack of detail on why each method failed, possible untried alternatives, and unknown plan criteria. The case could go either way depending on these gaps.
